articles.title: Could a redevelopment authority solve Cook County's vacant lot problem?
articles.text:
Could a redevelopment authority solve Cook County's vacant lot problem? - WBEZ Chicago
Cook County Commissioner Bridget Gainer at vacant lots near the former U.S. Steel South Works steel mill site at the 8800 block of South Baltimore Avenue. Gainer has led community workshops exploring ways to redevelop thousands of vacant lots across Cook County, including a proposal to establish a redevelopment authority.
Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times
Real Estate & Development
Could a redevelopment authority solve Cook County's vacant lot problem?
More than 100 Chicago leaders gathered for a series of workshops to discuss possible solutions for the thousands of vacant lots in Cook County.
By
Abby Miller
[month] [day], [year], [hour]:[minute][ampm] [timezone]
SHARE
COPY LINK
Share
Email
Facebook
Twitter
Bluesky
Print
A group of Chicago leaders recently came up with some ideas for repurposing the estimated 50,000 vacant lots scattered across Cook County: an Englewood tree ribbon, community farms and gardens and new housing near South Chicago’s quantum computing campus.
The proposals were part of a series of workshops, or so-called charrettes, where participants such as developers, funders, artists and more discussed possible solutions for the thousands of vacant lots in the county. Their ideas were presented at the Chicago Architecture Center last month at an event called “The Future is on the Map.”
The charrettes hosted 175 leaders from around the Chicago area at the Obama Presidential Center in September to discuss three areas that the vacant lots could support: arts, culture and open space; housing; and economic development. Attendees included Chicago Transit Authority Acting President Nora Leerhsen and Michael Fassnacht, Clayco’s chief growth officer and former CEO of World Business Chicago.
Ghian Foreman, president and CEO of the Emerald South Economic Development Collaborative and an attendee, said they came up with fresh ideas that included a range of perspectives.
“It was Chicago. It wasn’t just the same people that I’m used to being in the room with saying the same things that we always say to each other,” Foreman said. “You had a cross-section of people across the city of Chicago, and everyone was able to put in a little bit of their expertise — like a potluck dinner. Everybody brought these ideas to the table.”
Also among the ideas was something that’s been floated in Chicago throughout the years: a redevelopment authority.
There are hundreds of redevelopment authorities across the U.S. At one point, there were 400 in California. The public agencies operate at either the local, county or state level and are tasked with acquiring and priming land for redevelopment as a way to reduce community blight. But no redevelopment authorities exist in Illinois, according to Cook County Commissioner Bridget Gainer.
“If you look around, whether it’s the city, the county, or the state, there is not one single entity that is responsible for producing housing at speed, at affordability and geographically distributed in communities all over,” Gainer said.
The Cook County Land Bank Authority was formed by the Cook County Board in 2013 to redevelop the large number of vacant properties in the county, from residential to commercial and industrial buildings. While the land bank has helped create roughly 3,000 homes, Gainer said it has a narrow scope for how it addresses vacancies and build new homes. As the state carves out agencies like the Northern Illinois Transit Authority, Gainer sees an opportunity to do something similar with housing.
Now, Gainer wants to lead the path to creating a redevelopment authority.
“The affordability of housing — it keeps people here. It grows our population. It allows people to have a dignified existence,” Gainer, who helped found the land bank, said. “It really behooves us to go out of our way to make it work.”
More planning
The Chicago region is just one place that has renewed interest in establishing redevelopment authorities. But interest in them is far and wide, said Justin Marlowe, director of the Center for Municipal Finance at the University of Chicago’s Harris School of Public Policy. He said it stems, in part, from the federal government pulling back funding for the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development.
“We typically thought about these sorts of redevelopment activities as having a lot of federal involvement, which is not to say that they don’t or that they won’t going forward,” Marlowe said. “But I think there’s lots of questions right now about what kind of partner the federal government is going to be when it comes to these sorts of urban development issues. And so you have lots of places now saying if we’re going to do this, we probably do need to muster the support to do it locally and regionally.”
Chicago owns 10,000 vacant lots and has taken several stabs at reducing that figure, including launching the Missing Middle Infill Housing program in 2024. The program, which sells vacant land to developers for $1, has created more than 300 new homes on the South and West sides, where vacant lots are the most prolific.
A redevelopment authority could advance the city’s work and the land bank’s efforts by putting tax entitlement clearance, debt writing capacity and development authority under one entity, Gainer said.
Vacant lots near the former U.S. Steel South Works site on the 8800 block of South Baltimore Avenue in South Chicago.
Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times
Emerald South, the Obama Foundation’s economic development partner, aims to attract and coordinate investment in neighborhoods such as Washington Park, Woodlawn and South Shore, with a focus on increasing local ownership and prosperity. Its $50 million Terra Firma program is designed to beautify, maintain and activate vacant land.

Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times

Judge denies pause on hemp THC product ban, prohibiting sale outside dispensaries
Any products with more than 0.4 milligrams of THC are now considered cannabis in Illinois and must be sold in a dispensary after Gov. JB Pritzker signed a bill that was then challenged by businesses and the Illinois Healthy Alternatives Association.
By
Mary Norkol
[month] [day], [year], [hour]:[minute][ampm] [timezone]
SHARE
COPY LINK
Share
Email

Twitter
Bluesky
Print
Hemp-infused THC products can no longer be purchased outside of dispensaries in Illinois after a judge upheld the original timeline of the ban Thursday.
Judge Martha Pacold denied a motion for a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction, which would have delayed the onset of the ban, filed by the Illinois Healthy Alternatives Association and several businesses that sell the products.
The ban, which was set to go into effect Thursday, would halt the sale of THC-infused drinks and edibles at gas stations, convenience stores and other retailers after Gov. JB Pritzker signed a bill reclassifying products with more than 0.4 milligrams of THC as cannabis, therefore prohibiting them sold outside of dispensaries.
ILHAA President Craig Katz said the organization is considering appealing the judge’s decision.
“We respectfully disagree with the judge’s decision,” he said in a statement. “We look forward to further pursuing our claims in the preliminary injunction. We are exploring review in the appellate court.”
Businesses who continue to sell hemp products risk fines and other enforcement by the state government.
Some Chicago businesses have warned they would have to close if the ban goes through.
“Hopefully, they extend it for a longer period of time,” South Loop Market owner Anas Masoud said when the ban was initially delayed. “Any little bit will be great. We’re all struggling.”
The next court date is scheduled for Dec. 15.

articles.title: 'It's like our living room': Montrose Saloon in Albany Park set to close after decades-long run
articles.text:
'It's like our living room': Montrose Saloon in Albany Park set to close after decades-long run - WBEZ Chicago
Jeffrey Orhn pours out a drink at Montrose Saloon at 2933 W. Montrose Ave. in Albany Park.
Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times
Food & Drink
'It's like our living room': Montrose Saloon in Albany Park set to close after decades-long run
After more than five decades, Montrose Saloon at 2933 W. Montrose Ave., will close its doors after the new year, the bar’s Facebook page announced Friday.
By
Zoe Singer
Updated
[month] [day], [year], [hour]:[minute][ampm] [timezone]
SHARE
COPY LINK
Share
Email
Facebook
Twitter
Bluesky
Print
All it took was one visit to Montrose Saloon for Brian Pudil, 65, and his wife to decide to move into the apartment next door. It was love at first drink.
Since then, and for the past 16 years, Pudil has gone to the bar about three or four times each week to connect with other Montrose regulars.
“It’s like our living room,” he said. “Most of us are very caring, intelligent people that are really community-minded and like to have fun”
After more than five decades, Montrose Saloon will close its doors after New Year’s Eve, the bar’s Facebook page announced Friday.
Pudil said some loyal patrons heard the news Thursday. One day later, hundreds of bar-goers and musicians flooded Montrose’s Facebook post with comments about their fond memories of and love for the venue.
Brian Pudil and his dog Luca at Montrose Saloon at 2933 W. Montrose Ave. in Albany Park.
Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times
“Word got out,” Pudil said while visiting the bar as part of his weekly routine on Friday. “I was bummed. I was depressed, kind of.”
With string lights and red velvet curtains behind the stage, Montrose is known as a hub where bands and musicians perform for loyal and energetic audiences. On nights without live music, patrons rely on the bar’s jukebox to play American hits ranging from rock and roll to jazz.
“When they’re playing in there, it’s just high energy. You’re in another world and just taken away from your everyday troubles,” Pudil said. “You’re in another dimension.”
The bar’s indoor space, covered with music albums and artists’ portraits, serves as a cozy spot for music lovers, while the bar’s outdoor patio operates as a family-friendly area, open to children and dogs.
According to the Saloon’s website, the Albany Park “bar on the corner” opened its doors in 1976, but those who know the bar best say Montrose has been around for decades longer.
“It opened in 1945 at least. I have a picture of a bartender behind the bar in 1945,” bartender Jeffrey Ohrn said, who has been working at Montrose since the late 1980s.
Ohrn, 77, said he felt “a little bit crushed” to see the bar shut down.
Owners Eric and Katherine Chial at Montrose Saloon at 2933 W. Montrose Ave. in Albany Park.
Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times
“I’ve been coming here for an awful long time,” he said, with tears swelling in his eyes. “My kids grew up here.”
Current owner Eric Chial said the bar, which does not serve food, only makes its money off alcohol because it does not profit from live music.
“It has become increasingly difficult to have a business run on that model,” he said. “We’ve never made any real money here.”
Montrose’s doors will be closed through the winter, the bar’s slowest season, while Chial and the management team consider potential new business models the bar could implement to reopen its doors in the future. What a new model could look like “remains an open question.”
Patrons sit at the bar at Montrose Saloon at 2933 W. Montrose Ave. in Albany Park, Friday, Nov. 20, 2026. | Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times
Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times
Montrose’s post said the primary goal was to build community. “From that standpoint, we consider the project a complete success.”
Even if the iconic pub shuts down permanently, Pudil said the friendships created at Montrose will remain strong.
“We’ll probably start going to other people’s homes. We already are doing that somewhat,” Pudil said. “There are other places in Chicago, but this had been here forever, and it was a good place.”
While hope for a reopening after the winter remains, Montrose concluded its official public announcement of its closing stating, “Montrose Saloon is dead. Long live Montrose Saloon.”
The stage where bands perform at Montrose Saloon at 2933 W. Montrose Ave. in Albany Park.
Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times
A photo of Montrose Saloon in the early 1900s that still hangs inside the bar today.

articles.title: The Rundown: What to know about the lead dust plume
articles.text:
The Rundown: What to know about the lead dust plume - WBEZ Chicago
A sign sits along the fence of the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant on Nov. 20, 2026 in Middletown, Iowa.
Scott Olson/Getty Images
The Rundown: WBEZ’s Daily Newsletter
The Rundown: What to know about the lead dust plume
Plus, the perfect Bridgeport bike ride. Here’s what you need to know today.
By
Bianca Cseke
[month] [day], [year], [hour]:[minute][ampm] [timezone]
SHARE
COPY LINK
Share
Email
Facebook
Twitter
Bluesky
Print
Good afternoon! It’s Friday, and another mild fall weekend awaits us. (Brace yourself for massive Christkindlmarket lines.) Here’s what else you need to know today.
1. The Army plans to detonate a toxic lead stockpile near the Illinois-Iowa border. Here’s what to know
The explosion is expected to create a dust plume containing lead that may cross into Illinois. Lead is toxic to humans and animals. Late last night, the Army moved the planned explosion from today to Monday after politicians from Iowa and Illinois asked for a delay. A fight in federal court could delay the detonation further. A U.S. appellate court temporarily blocked the explosion until it fully considers environmental groups’ request to halt it.
There’s a risk these stored materials will detonate on their own, and moving them could also trigger an explosion, according to the Defense Department. The issue was discovered earlier this year, and plans to blow up the materials have been ongoing for months.
Illinois Environmental Protection Agency officials say based on current air modeling conducted by the U.S. Army, the dust cloud from the detonation could come close to Mercer County in Illinois. It’s unclear if the lead dust could blow as far northeast as Chicago. The Army will update its models before and after the detonation, which could change which Illinois communities might be affected.
The Illinois Department of Public Health recommends staying indoors and keeping windows closed for 24 to 48 hours after the detonation. If you have an HVAC system that actively draws in outside air, such as a school or commercial building, you may want to temporarily close the intake and switch to recirculate. If you need to drive through an area impacted by dust, set your car’s AC/heater to recirculate. Afterward, you can take your car to the car wash and replace the cabin filter.
Other safety tips include using a portable air cleaner to supplement your furnace filter, cleaning outdoor surfaces when you see visible dust using soap and water, and washing your hands before eating and drinking and taking your shoes off at the entrance when you enter your home. [ Chicago Sun-Times/WBEZ/Grist]
2. Who gets booted in Chicago? Drivers on the South and West sides are hit especially hard
The city’s booting program — immobilization, as city officials call it — was established in 1987. The threat that drivers with delinquent traffic tickets might find one of the yellow metal devices latched onto one of their vehicle’s wheels to make it undriveable was meant to make them pay up.
Drivers in some parts of the South Side and the West Side got booted at rates twice the citywide rate, my colleague Nicole Jeanine Johnson reports. Those neighborhoods include Englewood, Oakland and West Garfield Park and portions of Austin, East Garfield Park, Humboldt Park and Woodlawn. The same areas are among communities with the highest number of drivers on the city’s boot list.
The median amount owed by booted drivers was about $650. The most owed? More than $106,000.
Critics of the program say the combination of automated enforcement, hefty ticket prices and mounting fees for delinquent traffic and parking tickets can easily exceed the ability of some drivers to be able to pay their debt. That lands them on the city’s boot list. Then the added fees they’ll face for the towing and impounding of their vehicles can overwhelm them financially, ensnaring them in a debt trap for months and sometimes years.
“These debts can spiral out of control really quickly and become quite invasive in a person’s life,” said Kasey Henricks, an assistant professor in the University of Illinois Chicago’s Department of Criminology, Law and Justice. “Literally taking people’s cars away is taking away their mobility in a place where their livelihood is dependent upon that. It completely devastates people’s lives if you have outstanding ticket debt in Chicago.” [ WBEZ/Chicago Sun-Times]
3. SNAP enrollment in Illinois keeps dropping in the wake of the ‘One Big Beautiful Bill’ overhaul
Participation in the federal food assistance program is at its lowest level since 2009, declining even among children under 18, according to new data from the Illinois Department of Human Services. That’s despite persistent food insecurity, my colleague Elvia Malagón reports.
By September, SNAP enrollment continued to decrease in Illinois to 1.4 million people, the lowest program participation since 2009. That amounts to about a 23% decrease in the number of people getting food assistance compared to last fall. And the future of the program remains uncertain.
Galvanized by Democrats gaining the majority in Congress, Gov. JB Pritzker issued a list of policy recommendations for federal lawmakers. Repealing SNAP eligibility restrictions and changing the state’s financial burden to administer the program were among Pritzker’s top policy recommendations. At the same time, the Trump administration is proposing another change to SNAP that could further shrink eligibility, the New York Times reported.
You can see a list of community groups distributing food ahead of Thanksgiving in the link. [ Chicago Sun-Times]
4. Evanston landmark officials look to save a modernist Chase bank from demolition
As Chicago Sun-Times architecture columnist Lee Bey reports, the northern suburb’s Preservation Commission voted in favor of pursuing landmark status for a modernist Chase bank branch designed by a disciple of Mies van der Rohe.

SNAP enrollment in Illinois keeps dropping in wake of 'One Big Beautiful Bill' overhaul
Participation in the federal food assistance program is at its lowest level since 2009, declining even among children under 18, according to new data from the Illinois Department of Human Services.
By
Elvia Malagón

Tucked into the corner of the basement of an Oak Park church, Aida Ayala worked on her laptop as she helped a woman sign up for federal food assistance during Beyond Hunger’s food distribution.
“Any help will be amazing,” the woman said to Ayala, adding that she was also behind on rent.
A partition separated Ayala’s workspace from a man demonstrating how to make pumpkin-flavored hummus to a group waiting to pick up groceries. Ayala, a benefit service coordinator for Beyond Hunger, made her way through the list of people trying to navigate the bureaucracy of safety-net programs like the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program.
One man wanted to know why he was only receiving $25 in SNAP benefits. Another woman wanted help getting a state identification card.
Aida Ayala, benefits service coordinator, offers free counseling on SNAP eligibility and access at the Beyond Hunger food pantry location in suburban Oak Park.
Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times
Even as food insecurity persists, the number of people receiving food assistance in Illinois continues to decrease months after the state predicted many would lose access due to expanded work rules imposed by H.R.1, more commonly known as the “One Big Beautiful Bill,” championed by President Donald Trump.
By September, SNAP enrollment continued to decrease in Illinois to 1.4 million people, the lowest program participation since 2009. That amounts to about a 23% decrease in the number of people getting food assistance compared to last fall. And the future of the program remains uncertain.
Galvanized by Democrats gaining the majority in Congress, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker issued a list of policy recommendations for federal lawmakers. Repealing SNAP eligibility restrictions and changing the state’s financial burden to administer the program were among Pritzker’s top policy recommendations. At the same time, the Trump administration is proposing another change to SNAP that could further shrink eligibility, the New York Times reported.
In Cook County, advocates are working to pinpoint what exactly is driving the enrollment decrease. Beyond adults expected to meet the expanded work requirements, participation in Cook County has also fallen among children and those 60 years and older compared from this summer to the fall, according to data from the state.
Yet, residents are still seeking out the program. In fact, the state received the most SNAP applications from Cook County residents in August and September compared to monthly data from the past two years, according to data from the Illinois Department of Human Services.
Margarita Muñoz, 56, of Cicero, was among those who applied for SNAP this year. She started receiving benefits in August but it was terminated by the next month for reasons she says are unclear.
Muñoz found the online application intimidating, but after completing a recent internship with Hunger Free America, she applied and got back on SNAP. She and her son, a sophomore at DePaul University, receive $25 a month in food assistance.
“Well, $25 is better than nothing,” Muñoz said.
Confusion leads to terminations
Earlier this year, Gwynne Kizer Mashon, associate director for the public benefits practice at Legal Aid Chicago, said lawyers got wind that a group of SNAP recipients living in a senior building planned to pull themselves voluntarily from the program because of the H.R. 1 rules. The group, which provides free legal aid, sent a paralegal to reassure the seniors living there that they could keep their benefits.
“We knew by the definition of them living there, they were exempt,” Kizer Mashon said, referencing the type of building where the seniors lived. “...They were going to proactively stop their SNAP benefits because they were so scared that if they kept their SNAP, that it would interfere with their social security benefits.”
It’s that type of confusion that could be driving some of the decline in enrollment, Kizer Mashon and other advocates said.
Congress last year expanded work rules to include 55- to 64-year-olds, veterans and parents whose youngest child is 14 years or older — a change from 18 and older. Individuals have to prove they work or volunteer 80 hours per month to continue getting benefits, but the state has implemented exemptions that would allow people to continue getting food assistance.
Some exemptions include earning at least $935 per month in gross income, experiencing chronic homelessness or being the main caretaker for an incapacitated or disabled person.
Lorena Alvarez, community engagement and benefits outreach coordinator, offers handouts to cars in the drive thru line outside the Beyond Hunger food pantry in suburban Oak Park.
Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times
Kizer Mashon said they’ve been successful in all but a handful of cases involving people seeking to regain food assistance after they’ve lost it. Legal Aid Chicago has trained pro bono attorneys in Chicago who are also helping people retain their benefits.

With less than a week before Thanksgiving, and just about a month before Christmas, Say More asks listeners to share their holiday horror stories. Callers tell tales of fights, chaos, food poisonings and gift gaffes. Mary and Pat ask folks to get their resentments off their chests so they can avoid shouting them out around the dinner table.
Plus, a psychologist explains why family resentments fester, and how to address elephants in the room without spoiling dinner or creating new problems.
GUEST: Jason Washburn, chief of psychology, psychiatry and behavioral sciences department, Feinberg School of Medicine
